```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nestedscales)
```

This vignette takes one object apart. The example is a small classification
of industries by business code, in the style of a statistical classification
of activities: sections (`C`, Manufacturing) hold divisions (`C10`, Food
products), which hold classes (`C101`). The codes, the names and every
number are invented for illustration and reproduce no official
classification. The example has every awkward feature: a code reused at two
frames, a frame that cross-cuts another, a leaf with no code at one frame,
and attributes stored at three different frames.

The cross-cutting frame is `size`, a grouping of the classes by the typical
size of their firms, `small` or `large`. Public administration (`O84`) is
not made of firms and has no size, and it is not subdivided, so its only
class carries the code of its division.

```{r industries}
lt <- data.frame(
  section  = c("C", "C", "C", "C", "C", "D", "D", "D", "O"),
  size     = c("small", "large", "small", "large", "large",
               "large", "small", "small", NA),
  division = c("C10", "C10", "C11", "C24", "C24",
               "D35", "D35", "D35", "O84"),
  class    = c("C101", "C102", "C110", "C241", "C242",
               "D351", "D352", "D353", "O84")
)
at <- data.frame(
  frame     = c("class", "class", "division", "section", "class", "division"),
  member    = c("C101", "C102", "D35", "C", "C241", "D35"),
  attribute = c("wage", "wage", "wage", "wage", "floor_area", "floor_area"),
  kind      = c(rep("property", 4), "factor", "factor"),
  value     = c(30, 28, 45, 32, 60, 20),
  unit_of_measure = c(rep("thousand/employee", 4), "m2/employee",
                      "m2/employee"),
  source    = "example"
)
al <- data.frame(
  frame  = c("class", "division", "class", "division", "division"),
  member = c("C101", "C10", "O84", "O84", "O84"),
  alias  = c("meat", "food", "public admin", "public admin", "government"),
  source = "example"
)
x <- scale_from_leaftable(
  lt, frames = c("section", "size", "division", "class"), leaf = "class",
  attributes = at, aliases = al, name = "industries"
)
x
```

## The object

A `NestedScale` is an S7 object with eight properties. `str()` lists them
with their size and purpose:

```{r props}
str(x)
```

The standard S7 tools apply: `S7::prop_names(x)` gives the names,
`x@frames` or `S7::prop(x, "frames")` reads one property, and
`S7::props(x)` returns all of them as a list.

```{r props-s7}
S7::prop_names(x)
x@frames
```

The object is a **definition**: the leaves, the frames that group them, and
the weights that say how big each leaf is. It never holds data. Data stays
in ordinary tables, and a table is tied to a scale by its code columns; see
[The data link](#the-data-link) below.

| property | type | holds |
|---|---|---|
| `leaftable` | `data.frame` | one row per leaf: one column per frame, the leaf column, weight columns |
| `frames` | `character` | the hierarchy, ordered coarsest first |
| `members` | named `list` | the ordered code vocabulary at each frame |
| `leaf` | `character` | the name of the leaf column (`"leaf"` by default) |
| `meta` | `list` | `name`, `desc`, `weights`, `default_weight`, and whatever the builder adds |
| `attributes` | `data.frame` | values keyed by `(frame, member)`: `attribute`, `kind`, `value`, `lower`, `upper`, `unit_of_measure`, `source`, `note` |
| `aliases` | `data.frame` | alternative spellings keyed by `(frame, member)`: `alias`, `source` |
| `labels` | `data.frame` | display names keyed by `(frame, member, variant)`: `label` |

Everything else -- parent/child tables, ancestry, shares, resolved
attributes -- is derived on demand; nothing is cached on the object. The
three tables are empty unless the builder fills them; a scale saved by an
earlier version, which had no such properties, loads and validates
unchanged.

## The leaftable

```{r leaftable}
scale_leaftable(x)
```

Each row is one leaf. The leaf column (`class` here) is unique and
complete. Frame columns may hold `NA`: `O84` has no firm size, so it does
not participate at the `size` frame, and `na_action=` decides what recasts
do about it. The leaf column may be the finest frame, as here: the frame
column *is* the leaf column.

## Frames, members, ranks

```{r frames}
scale_frames(x)
scale_leaf_frame(x)                # the finest frame, or the leaf column
scale_members(x, "division")       # the members at one frame
scale_members(x)                   # the leaves
scale_rank(x, "division")
```

Codes are **not unique across frames**: `O84` is a division and a class
here. Every function that takes a code therefore takes its frame as well.

Navigation is derived from the leaftable and routed through the leaves, so a
frame that cross-cuts another reports overlap rather than invented
containment:

```{r navigate}
scale_nests(x, "division", "class")  # a tree
scale_nests(x, "size", "division")   # C10 and D35 are small and large
scale_parents(x, "division", "D35", target = "size")
scale_ancestors(x, "class", "D352")
scale_descendants(x, "section", "C")
head(scale_ancestry(x), 4)
```

## The attribute table

Attributes live in one long table, and a row may sit on **any** member, not
only on a leaf. Here a wage per employee is given for two classes, one
division and one section, and a floor area per employee for one class and
one division:

```{r attributes}
scale_attributes(x)
```

Reading with a `frame` resolves one value per member, walking to the
nearest coarser frame when a member has none of its own, and says where the
value came from:

```{r resolve}
scale_attributes(x, "wage", frame = "class")[
  c("member", "value", "unit_of_measure", "origin_frame", "origin_member")]
```

Attributes are **not weights**. A weight says how big a leaf is and drives
aggregation; an attribute is a per-member conversion factor and is consumed
only by `convert_scale()`. The constructor promotes numeric leaftable
columns to weights, so a wage must be passed as `attributes=`, never as a
leaftable column. Every attribute name carries a `kind`: `property` (an
invertible ratio) or `factor` (one-way).

```{r kinds}
SCALE_ATTRIBUTE_KINDS
```

`vignette("attributes")` has the reasoning and the full account of
inheritance, sources and conversion.

## The alias table

The members of this scale are codes; the alias table holds the names and
spellings by which other tables refer to the same activities.

```{r aliases}
scale_aliases(x)
scale_match(x, c("meat", "Public Admin", "C242"))
```

One alias may point at several members (`public admin` above); matching
reports that as ambiguous unless `frame=` narrows it. Matching is exact and
case-insensitive, with no fuzzy stage.

## The label table

Labels are display names. A label belongs to a member and to a named
*variant*, so one member may carry a full name, a short one and a
translation, while another frame carries none at all and is shown by its
codes. A row with `member = NA` names the frame itself. The divisions get
two variants here, a short name and a long one, and the short one is
declared the default:

```{r labels}
x <- attach_labels_scale(
  x,
  data.frame(
    frame   = "division",
    member  = rep(c("C10", "C24", "O84", NA), 2),
    variant = rep(c("short", "long"), each = 4),
    label   = c("Food", "Metals", "Administration", "Division",
                "Manufacture of food products",
                "Manufacture of basic metals",
                "Public administration", "Division of activity")
  ),
  default = "short"
)
scale_labels(x)
scale_label(x, c("C10", "C11", "O84"), frame = "division")
scale_label(x, c("C10", "C11", "O84"), frame = "division", variant = "long")
scale_label(x, scale_members(x, "size"), frame = "size")   # no labels: codes
```

`C11` has no label in either variant and is shown by its code. Aliases and
labels serve different purposes. An alias is a spelling to be *recognised*
(`scale_match()`); a label is a name to be *shown* (`scale_label()`,
`join_scale(labels = )`).

## Weights and meta

```{r meta}
scale_weights(x)                        # none declared here
S7::prop(x, "meta")[c("name", "desc")]
```

`meta$name` is load-bearing: `join_scale()` prefixes the columns it attaches
with `"<name>."`, `scale_map_between()` names its label columns after the
objects, and `write_scale()` needs a name for the definition. Further
fields passed to the constructor are kept in `meta` as given.

## The data link

A table of data is tied to a scale by its code columns. Unbound, the tie is
the column name alone: a column called `division` is read as codes at the
`division` frame. Two scales can share frame names and codes, so the name
does not say *which* scale the data is on. `bind_scale()` records it on the
column itself, together with the scale's identity. The link is
experimental: it is lost when the column is converted to a factor or a
plain character vector, and it may change.

```{r link}
scale_id(x)
d <- data.frame(class = scale_members(x), jobs = seq_along(scale_members(x)))
b <- bind_scale(d, x)
scale_link(b)
```

`scale_id()` is the scale's name plus a hash of its structure -- leaf column,
frames and memberships. Weights, attributes, aliases and labels do not enter, so
enriching a scale does not detach the data bound to it; a subset or a
re-grouping is a different scale.

A bound column is still a character vector. It keeps the link through row
subsetting, `mutate()`, grouping, joins and row binding, and the verbs use
it: the source frame is taken from the link, the result is bound to the
target frame, and data bound to another scale is refused.

```{r link-verbs}
register_scale_rule("jobs", "sum")
out <- recast_scale(b, x, target = "division")
scale_link(out)
clear_scale_rules("jobs")
```

Unbound data behaves as before, and its results stay unbound. A lazy table
(arrow, dtplyr) cannot carry the link in memory; `write_scale_dataset()`
records it in the store and `scale_link()` reads it back.

## What the validator guarantees

`scale_from_leaftable()` and every operation that rebuilds a scale enforce:

- the leaf column is present, unique and complete; every frame is a
  leaftable column and `members` are exactly its non-`NA` values, in a
  stable order;
- weights are numeric and finite;
- every attribute and alias row names a `(frame, member)` that is a member;
  `value` is finite; `lower <= value <= upper` where given; `kind` is one
  of `SCALE_ATTRIBUTE_KINDS` and one attribute name has one kind;
  `unit_of_measure` and `source` are non-empty; no duplicate
  `(frame, member, attribute, source)` rows and no duplicate alias rows.

The order of `frames` is a convention, coarsest first; the
direction-dependent rules (`share`, residuals, reconciliation) follow it.

Subsetting keeps the tables consistent: `filter_scale()` and `[` keep the
attribute and alias rows of every surviving member at every frame, and
`prune_scale()` keeps the rows at the frames that survive the collapse.

```{r subset}
manufacturing <- x["section", "C"]
scale_attributes(manufacturing)[c("frame", "member", "attribute", "value")]
```

`prune_scale()` needs the frames above the new leaf frame to nest, so the
cross-cutting `size` has to go first:

```{r prune}
tree <- scale_from_leaftable(
  lt[c("section", "division", "class")],
  frames = c("section", "division", "class"),
  leaf = "class", attributes = at, aliases = al, name = "tree"
)
scale_aliases(prune_scale(tree, "division"))
```

## Definition files

A scale is stored as a definition, not as an R object: a JSON header with
the three tables inline, or, for large scales, a `<name>.scale/` bundle
directory holding the header and the tables as Arrow IPC or CSV files. The
Python binding reads and writes the same files.

```{r definition}
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "industries.json")
write_scale(x, path)
cat(head(readLines(path), 12), sep = "\n")
back <- read_scale(path)
identical(scale_frames(back), scale_frames(x))
identical(scale_attributes(back), scale_attributes(x))
```

`write_scale(format = "yaml")` writes the same header as YAML, and
`read_scale()` accepts either. Installed packages register directories of
definitions; `scale_catalog()` lists them and `read_scale(id)` opens one by
its id:

```{r catalog}
scale_catalog()[c("id", "name", "kind", "frames", "n_leaves", "package")]
```

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(path)
```

## The registry

One package-level registry changes behaviour explicitly. **Rules** map
value-column names to their aggregation rule; there is no fallback, and an
unregistered column without `rule=` is an error:

```{r rules}
SCALE_RULES
register_scale_rule("jobs", "sum")
register_scale_rule("wage", "weighted_mean", weight = "jobs")
get_scale_rule("wage")
list_scale_rules()
clear_scale_rules()
```

A rule may be scoped to one dimension with `scope=`, so a `jobs` column
aggregates the same way over industries, regions and months without being
registered three times -- or differently, when it should.
